hypothesis: If Darwin is right that domestic dogs descend from several distinct wild species (he had in mind wolves and jackals), then some domestic dog maternal lineages should trace to a wild canid species other than the grey wolf: a non-trivial fraction of dog mitochondrial genomes should be closer to Canis aureus, C. lupaster, C. latrans, C. simensis, Cuon alpinus or Lycaon pictus than to any wild Canis lupus.
pass_criterion: Using complete mitochondrial genomes from GenBank (a systematic one-in-three sample of all 'Canis lupus familiaris' records, every wild 'Canis lupus' record, and every record of the other wild canid species), with CYTB and COX1 coding sequences extracted and compared by ungapped p-distance: at least 3 dog sequences AND at least 2 % of sampled dog sequences have their nearest non-dog sequence in a species other than Canis lupus. That outcome supports a multi-species origin.
fail_criterion: Zero dog sequences are nearer to a non-wolf species than to wild wolves: refutes (every maternal lineage sampled is wolf-derived). One or two such sequences (consistent with mislabelled hybrids) or the per-cent threshold unmet: mixed. If fewer than 100 dog sequences or fewer than 20 wild wolf sequences can be retrieved and parsed: inconclusive (underpowered).
interpretation: Darwin's 'several wild species' is read as more than one wild canid species contributing ancestry to domestic dogs. The species Darwin would have counted (wolf, jackals, coyote, dhole, African wild dog, Ethiopian wolf) are the wild canids with GenBank mitogenomes. Mitochondrial DNA tests maternal ancestry only; if even the maternal lineages are exclusively wolf-derived, the multi-species claim is refuted for the component that pre-genomic data can address, and nuclear genomic literature is cited in caveats but is not used as data. Dingoes and 'Canis lupus dingo' records are reported separately and excluded from the dog sample; records of 'Canis lupus' other than familiaris and dingo are treated as wild wolves (GenBank labels, which can include captive or admixed animals, are taken at face value). Modern taxonomy already files the dog inside Canis lupus, which the test does not assume.
